title: Energy Bands in Solids
notes: When many atoms form a solid, interactions split atomic energy levels into closely spaced allowed bands separated by forbidden energy gaps. Electrons cannot occupy energies in an ideal band gap.
The valence band contains bonding electrons; the conduction band contains mobile carriers. The gap Eg=Ec−Ev and the band filling help explain conductivity.

### Deep dive: bands, gaps and the conductor/insulator switch

When N atoms bond into a solid, each atomic level splits into N closely spaced levels — effectively a continuous *band*. The valence band holds the bonding electrons; the conduction band is the first empty band where electrons can move freely. What separates them is the *forbidden gap* $E_g$, and its width decides everything: conductors have overlapping bands (no gap), insulators have huge gaps (diamond ≈ 5.5 eV), and semiconductors have small gaps (silicon ≈ 1.1 eV) that thermal energy at room temperature can occasionally bridge — which is why a semiconductor conducts a little, and conducts far more when heated or doped. Resistance *falls* with temperature in a semiconductor, the opposite of a metal.

**Band pictures of the three classes**

| Class | Band situation | Gap Eg | Behaviour with T |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conductor | valence and conduction overlap | none | resistance rises (metal) |
| Semiconductor | small gap between bands | ≈ 1 eV (Si 1.1) | resistance falls |
| Insulator | large gap | > 3 eV (diamond 5.5) | stays non-conducting |

**Band-gap energies at 300 K**

| Material | Eg (eV) | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Ge | 0.66 | early transistors, IR detectors |
| Si | 1.12 | workhorse of electronics |
| GaAs | 1.43 | LEDs, lasers |
| Diamond | 5.5 | insulator / UV optics |

Metals have partially filled bands or overlapping bands. Insulators have a large gap and very few room-temperature carriers. Semiconductors have a smaller gap, so thermal or optical excitation can promote electrons into the conduction band.
In an intrinsic semiconductor, promoting an electron leaves a hole in the valence band. Both the electron and the hole can carry current; heating can therefore increase carrier concentration.
A photon can excite an electron across the gap if hν≥Eg. This underlies photoconductivity and semiconductor photodetectors.

In a solid the atomic levels spread into bands. A conductor has a partly filled band, or overlapping bands, so electrons can take a little extra energy and move. An insulator has a full valence band and a large gap. A semiconductor has a smaller gap, so heat or light can lift a few electrons across it.

exercises.question: Silicon's gap is about 1.1 eV. A photon of wavelength 800 nm has energy 1240/800 = 1.55 eV. Can it lift an electron across the gap?
steps: 1.55 is greater than 1.1, so the photon can be absorbed and create a pair.
A photon of energy 0.9 eV could not.
Temperature can also free a few electrons without a photon.
exercises.answer: Yes. 1.55 eV is above the 1.1 eV gap.
